meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas. doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.title: Genome sequencing identifies a basis for everolimus sensitivity
data.authors: Iyer G; Solit DB et al.

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Genome sequencing of a single exceptional everolimus responder implicates TSC1 loss as the sensitivity basis. An n-of-1 observation, hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.
data.abstract_excerpt: Cancer drugs often induce dramatic responses in a small minority of patients. We used whole-genome sequencing to investigate the genetic basis of a durable remission of metastatic bladder cancer in a patient treated with everolimus, a drug that inhibits the mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) signaling pathway. Among the somatic mutations was a loss-of-function mutation in TSC1 (tuberous sclerosis complex 1), a regulator of mTOR pathway activation.

extracted_findings.species: Human – metastatic bladder cancer patient + tumor sequencing
extracted_findings.effect: Loss-of-function TSC1 mutation explains an exceptional everolimus response; TSC1 mutated in ~8% of bladder cancers
extracted_findings.dose: Everolimus (mTOR inhibitor) in a phase II trial; whole-genome/targeted tumor sequencing of an exceptional responder.
extracted_findings.sample_size: 1 exceptional responder + targeted sequencing of additional bladder tumors; 3 further TSC1-nonsense tumors identified (2 minor responders: 17% and 24% regression; 1 with 7%).
extracted_findings.effect_size: Loss-of-function TSC1 mutation underlies the exceptional everolimus response. TSC1-mutant tumors stayed on everolimus longer (7.7 vs 2.0 months, p=0.004) with improved time to recurrence (4.1 vs 1.8 months).
extracted_findings.limitations: Inference from rare responders; basis of mTOR-inhibitor sensitivity beyond TSC1/2 loss still incompletely understood.
